facts.claim: delivering the agent to the brain alone hardly changed the dose needed to stop movement
facts.problem: Misleading rendering of the classic goat bypass experiments. When isoflurane was delivered preferentially to the brain (torso receiving little), the brain concentration needed to prevent movement rose sharply, roughly 2.5 times the whole-body value; it was varying the brain's share while the torso was dosed normally that hardly changed the requirement. The conclusion the passage draws (immobility is mostly spinal) is correct, but the stated result inverts the key finding. The spinal-transection half of the sentence is accurate.
